statement: Where the Exchange creates or collects personally identifiable information for the purposes of determining eligibility for enrollment in a qualified health plan; determining eligibility for other insurance affordability programs, as defined in § 155.300; or determining eligibility for exemptions from the individual shared responsibility provisions in section 5000A of the Code, the Exchange may only use or disclose such personally identifiable information to the extent such information is necessary: (i) For the Exchange to carry out the functions described in § 155.200; (ii) For the Exchange to carry out other functions not described in paragraph (a)(1)(i) of this section, which the Secretary determines to be in compliance with section 1411(g)(2)(A) of the Affordable Care Act and for which an individual provides consent for his or her information to be used or disclosed; or (iii) For the Exchange to carry out other functions not described in paragraphs (a)(1)(i) and (ii) of this section, for which an individual provides consent for his or her information to be used or disclosed, and which the Secretary determines are in compliance with section 1411(g)(2)(A) of the Affordable Care Act under the following substantive and procedural requirements:

To seek approval for a use or disclosure of personally identifiable information created or collected as described in paragraph (a)(1) of this section that is not described in paragraphs (a)(1)(i) or (ii) of this section, the Exchange must submit the following information to HHS: (1) Identity of the Exchange and appropriate contact persons; (2) Detailed description of the proposed use or disclosure, which must include, but not necessarily be limited to, a listing or description of the specific information to be used or disclosed and an identification of the persons or entities that may access or receive the information; (3) Description of how the use or disclosure will ensure the efficient operation of the Exchange consistent with section 1411(g)(2)(A) of the Affordable Care Act; and (4) Description of how the information to be used or disclosed will be protected in compliance with privacy and security standards that meet the requirements of this section or other relevant law, as applicable.
The Exchange may not create, collect, use, or disclose personally identifiable information unless the creation, collection, use, or disclosure is consistent with this section.
Individuals should be provided with a simple and timely means to access and obtain their personally identifiable information in a readable form and format;

Individuals should be provided with a timely means to dispute the accuracy or integrity of their personally identifiable information and to have erroneous information corrected or to have a dispute documented if their requests are denied;
There should be openness and transparency about policies, procedures, and technologies that directly affect individuals and/or their personally identifiable information;
Individuals should be provided a reasonable opportunity and capability to make informed decisions about the collection, use, and disclosure of their personally identifiable information;
Personally identifiable information should be created, collected, used, and/or disclosed only to the extent necessary to accomplish a specified purpose(s) and never to discriminate inappropriately;

Persons and entities should take reasonable steps to ensure that personally identifiable information is complete, accurate, and up-to-date to the extent necessary for the person's or entity's intended purposes and has not been altered or destroyed in an unauthorized manner;

Personally identifiable information should be protected with reasonable operational, administrative, technical, and physical safeguards to ensure its confidentiality, integrity, and availability and to prevent unauthorized or inappropriate access, use, or disclosure; and,
These principles should be implemented, and adherence assured, through appropriate monitoring and other means and methods should be in place to report and mitigate non-adherence and breaches.
The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of personally identifiable information created, collected, used, and/or disclosed by the Exchange;
Personally identifiable information is only used by or disclosed to those authorized to receive or view it;
Return information, as such term is defined by section 6103(b)(2) of the Code, is kept confidential under section 6103 of the Code;
Personally identifiable information is protected against any reasonably anticipated threats or hazards to the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of such information;
Personally identifiable information is protected against any reasonably anticipated uses or disclosures of such information that are not permitted or required by law; and
Personally identifiable information is securely destroyed or disposed of in an appropriate and reasonable manner and in accordance with retention schedules;
The Exchange must monitor, periodically assess, and update the security controls and related system risks to ensure the continued effectiveness of those controls.
The Exchange must develop and utilize secure electronic interfaces when sharing personally identifiable information electronically.
A description of the functions to be performed by the non-Exchange entity;

A provision(s) binding the non-Exchange entity to comply with the privacy and security standards and obligations adopted in accordance with paragraph (b)(3) of this section, and specifically listing or incorporating those privacy and security standards and obligations;

A provision requiring the non-Exchange entity to monitor, periodically assess, and update its security controls and related system risks to ensure the continued effectiveness of those controls in accordance with paragraph (a)(5) of this section;
A provision requiring the non-Exchange entity to inform the Exchange of any change in its administrative, technical, or operational environments defined as material within the contract; and

A provision that requires the non-Exchange entity to bind any downstream entities to the same privacy and security standards and obligations to which the non-Exchange entity has agreed in its contract or agreement with the Exchange.

Be consistent with the principles and requirements listed in paragraphs (a)(1) through (6) of this section, including being at least as protective as the standards the Exchange has established and implemented for itself in compliance with paragraph (a)(3) of this section;
Comply with the requirements of paragraphs (c), (d), (f), and (g) of this section; and

Take into specific consideration: (A) The environment in which the non-Exchange entity is operating; (B) Whether the standards are relevant and applicable to the non-Exchange entity's duties and activities in connection with the Exchange; and (C) Any existing legal requirements to which the non-Exchange entity is bound in relation to its administrative, technical, and operational controls and practices, including but not limited to, its existing data handling and information technology processes and protocols.
The Exchange must ensure its workforce complies with the policies and procedures developed and implemented by the Exchange to comply with this section.
Be in writing, and available to the Secretary of HHS upon request; and
Identify applicable law governing collection, use, and disclosure of personally identifiable information.
Meet any applicable requirements described in this section;
Meet any applicable requirements described in section 1413(c)(1) and (c)(2) of the Affordable Care Act;
Be equal to or more stringent than the requirements for Medicaid programs under section 1942 of the Act; and
For those matching agreements that meet the definition of “matching program” under 5 U.S.C. 552a(a)(8), comply with 5 U.S.C. 552a(o).
Return information, as defined in section 6103(b)(2) of the Code, must be kept confidential and disclosed, used, and maintained only in accordance with section 6103 of the Code.

The Board is ultimately responsible for information security and ensures it is maintained commensurate with the size and extent of threats, enabling continued sound operation
Information security roles and responsibilities of the Board, senior management, governing bodies and individuals (decision-making, approval, oversight, operations) are clearly defined
An information security capability commensurate with the size and extent of threats to information assets is maintained
The information security capability of each related party or third party managing information assets is assessed, commensurate with the potential consequences of an incident
The capability is actively maintained against changes in vulnerabilities and threats, including from changes to information assets or the business environment
An information security policy framework commensurate with exposures to vulnerabilities and threats is maintained
The policy framework provides direction on the responsibilities of all parties obliged to maintain information security (staff, contractors, consultants, related and third parties, customers)
Information assets, including those managed by related and third parties, are classified by criticality and sensitivity reflecting the potential financial and non-financial impact of an incident

Information security controls protect information assets, implemented in a timely manner and commensurate with vulnerabilities and threats, criticality and sensitivity, life-cycle stage, and the potential consequences of an incident
The design of each related party's or third party's information security controls protecting the entity's information assets is evaluated
Robust mechanisms detect and respond to information security incidents in a timely manner
Information security response plans are maintained for incidents that could plausibly occur
Response plans include mechanisms for managing all stages from detection to post-incident review, and for escalation and reporting to the Board, governing bodies and responsible individuals
Information security response plans are reviewed and tested annually to ensure they remain effective and fit-for-purpose

Control effectiveness is tested through a systematic testing program whose nature and frequency match the rate of change in threats, asset criticality and sensitivity, incident consequences, exposure to untrusted environments, and the materiality and frequency of change
Where reliance is placed on a related party's or third party's control testing, the nature and frequency of that testing is assessed against paragraph 27(a)–(e)
Testing results that identify control deficiencies which cannot be remediated in a timely manner are escalated and reported to the Board or senior management
Testing is conducted by appropriately skilled and functionally independent specialists
The sufficiency of the testing program is reviewed at least annually or on material change to information assets or the business environment
Internal audit reviews the design and operating effectiveness of information security controls, including those maintained by related and third parties (control assurance)
Information security control assurance is provided by appropriately skilled personnel
Internal audit assesses control assurance provided by a related or third party where an incident could materially affect the entity or its customers and audit intends to rely on that assurance

APRA is notified as soon as possible and no later than 72 hours after becoming aware of an information security incident that materially affected (or could materially affect) the entity or its customers, or that was notified to another regulator
APRA is notified as soon as possible and no later than 10 business days after becoming aware of a material control weakness the entity expects not to remediate in a timely manner

RMiT 11.4 — whether the institution is designated a National Critical Information Infrastructure entity under the Cyber Security Act 2024 must be declared true or false

Technology project governance is commensurate with risk and complexity: oversight roles, authority and reporting structures, and risk assessments throughout the project life cycle
Changes to source code of critical systems undergo source code review for security and recognised coding practices before introduction
System changes are independently reviewed and approved; contingency plans for unsuccessful material changes are established and tested

Contracts for critical systems developed or maintained by third parties require sufficient notice of impacting changes, demonstrated secure-by-design development, and continued accessibility of source code for business continuity
Decommissioning of critical systems minimises customer and business impact, with contingency plans established and tested for unsuccessful decommissioning
Robust policies identify and reduce shadow IT risks

No system or digital service runs with known security vulnerabilities, on outdated platforms or end-of-life technology: a current security hardening baseline, timely patching, remedial plans for approaching EOL, and management-approved, risk-assessed, annually reviewed exceptions with phase-out timelines

A patch and EOL management framework covers asset identification and risk assessment, deployment criteria, priority and turnaround by severity, compatibility testing, an end-to-end approval, testing, monitoring and tracking workflow, and end-user awareness

The effectiveness and security of technology in use is monitored against disruptive developments (e.g. quantum computing): board advice on impact, a long-term strategy with competent resources, and a migration roadmap

Project risk assessments address resource adequacy including vendors and concurrent projects, system complexity and integration, security controls through the life cycle, completeness of user requirements, robustness of testing, deployment and fallback strategies, and disaster recovery readiness

A cryptography policy requires industry-standard algorithms, message authentication, hashes, signatures and random number generation; secure key life-cycle management; at least annual review of standards and algorithms for critical and customer-facing systems; an asset inventory of cryptographic tools and algorithms with rationale and mappings; and tested compromise-recovery plans

Cryptographic controls are evaluated with due diligence; the institution retains ownership and control of encryption keys (or with an independent custodian) except for non-critical systems without customer information, manages externally generated keys to industry standards, weighs reliance on third-party assessments against risk appetite, and considers resource impact and reduced traffic visibility

Cryptographic protocols for secret and public keys follow recognised international standards and are tested; secret and private key storage and computation occur in a protected environment (HSM, TEE or equivalent) commensurate with risk

Public keys are stored in certificates from a Certificate Authority (recognised CAs for customers); authentication and signature protocols protect private keys so their use is legally binding; issuance and renewal follow industry and legal specifications
Resilience and availability objectives of data centres are specified to support business recovery objectives
Data centres have redundant capacity components and multiple distribution paths with no single point of failure

Critical systems are hosted in dedicated, physically secured production data centre space not in a disaster-prone area, with no single point of failure in hardware, electrical, thermal and infrastructure design, and with adequate maintenance and continuous monitoring with timely alerts
Data centre operations have control procedures including automated batch management, production change procedures, error handling and exception management
Incompatible activities in data centre operations are segregated (development from operations); necessary vendor or programmer access to production is authorised and monitored
System capacity is planned and managed for peak periods, growth plans and architecture changes
The board and senior management receive and review timely reports on significant project risks throughout implementation
Real-time monitoring tracks capacity utilisation and performance of key processes and services with actionable alerts; scope, metrics and thresholds are updated periodically

Key digital services and delivery channels are made resilient: early-warning mechanisms by 30 September 2027 (detect failed transactions and measure availability, monitor affected customers and volumes, escalate immediately when 5% or more of expected daily customers or transactions are affected), regular reviews of vulnerable interdependencies, and stand-in processing arrangements by 30 September 2027 prioritised for the least substitutable channels with customers informed of terms, risks and responsibilities

Critical systems with an expectation of immediate customer or counterparty service are designed for high availability: cumulative unplanned downtime at the customer interface of not more than 4 hours on a rolling 12 months and a maximum tolerable downtime of 120 minutes per incident
Diversity in technology is prioritised so critical systems infrastructure is not excessively exposed to similar technology risks

During digital service interruptions the institution escalates and decides promptly to resume via alternatives within the 10.32 timeframe, defines accountabilities and third-party arrangements for degradation, runs a communication plan with immediate customer notice, feedback handling, frequent updates and alternatives, offers a convenient availability-status check (e.g. real-time status on the website), and discloses its quarterly availability track record within 15 calendar days of quarter-end from 15 October 2027
A reliable, scalable and secure enterprise network supports business activities and growth plans
Network services for critical systems are reliable with no single point of failure against network faults and cyber threats
Real-time bandwidth monitoring and network resilience metrics flag over-utilisation and disruptions from congestion and faults, including traffic analysis for trends and anomalies

An enterprise technology architecture framework gives a comprehensive view of technology and baseline components, a technical design showing infrastructure, interconnectivity, dependencies and security controls (to find single points of failure), mappings to business functions, units, applications and data, principles for network and security design, and longer-term priorities
Network services supporting critical systems ensure confidentiality, integrity and availability of data
A maintained network design blueprint identifies all internal and external interfaces and connectivity, physical and logical, with segmentation
Sufficient network device logs are retained for investigation and forensics for at least three years
Safeguards (e.g. logical network segmentation from other group entities) minimise the risk of a compromise in one entity affecting others in the group

A backup strategy and procedures manage the backup life cycle, keep adequate copies of critical data, OS, programs, utilities, master and transaction files and event logs, store media in an environmentally secure access-controlled site, secure removable media per Appendix 1, test restoration periodically with prompt root-cause remediation, and have an independent risk assessment of end-to-end backup storage and delivery
A tamper-proof backup arrangement and an isolated recovery environment enable resumption of critical banking and payment services within tolerance after destructive cyber attacks such as ransomware
The board and senior management exercise effective oversight of third-party service providers for critical technology functions; the institution remains accountable for all resulting risks
Due diligence on third-party service providers is conducted before on-boarding and throughout the engagement, considering at least the Appendix 8 risks

Service level agreements with third-party providers include regulator and institution access rights to records and decision minutes, prior notice of substantial sub-contracting, a secrecy undertaking surviving the engagement, disaster recovery and backup, uptime objectives, exit and termination continuity with timely data recovery, prompt disclosure of disruptions and cyber incidents in the provider's or sub-contractors' environment, compliance with international standards and staff certification, and participation in security awareness programmes

A roadmap achieves continuous monitoring of third-party cybersecurity posture: measuring the infrastructure footprint and customer information accessible to third parties, leading product-specific controls, incident response protocols with providers for software-update vulnerabilities, a priority set of controls with frequent assurance assertions, higher-frequency monitoring of disclosed incidents, automated metric testing, and response to breached thresholds

An SDLC methodology covers requirement, design, development, testing, deployment, change management, maintenance and decommissioning, integrated with enterprise architecture, risk management and security principles including segregation of duties

A comprehensive risk assessment precedes cloud adoption, addressing deployment model sophistication, migration, infrastructure location and geopolitical and legal risk, multi-tenancy and data co-mingling, lock-in and portability, security configurability, exposure via the provider, termination and data recovery, demarcation of responsibilities and liability, and continuing regulatory and standards compliance

Customer, counterparty and proprietary data on cloud services are safeguarded against unauthorised disclosure and access, with ownership, control and management of all such data and services retained, including cryptographic key management
An access control policy governs identification, authentication and authorisation of all users to IT assets and data, with granularity commensurate with unauthorised-access risk

Access control adheres to deny-all by default, least privilege on a need-to-have basis, time-bound access, segregation of incompatible functions (development vs operations, security vs system administration, network operation vs network security, IT operations), dual-authorisation criteria, and authentication by criticality: stronger for critical activities and remote access, robust identity verification at provisioning, and credentials uniquely linked to one user
Multi-factor authentication resistant to social engineering, combining two or more of knowledge, inherent and possession factors, authenticates user access to critical systems
A user access matrix outlines access rights, roles or profiles and the authorising and approving authorities, reviewed and updated periodically

Access controls to enterprise-wide systems are managed and monitored, anomalies are flagged for prompt investigation, and user activities in critical systems are logged, retained at least three years and reviewed in a timely manner

Rapid development (DevOps) meets enterprise security, governance and compliance requirements, with automated IT security compliance review and automated vulnerability discovery and testing before release
Production is physically segregated from development and testing; on cloud, these environments do not run on the same virtual host
Rigorous system testing precedes deployment, verifying user requirements and robustness; sensitive test data requires authorisation and disclosure safeguards
Cyber risk management has an enterprise-wide focus reflecting the collective responsibility of business and technology lines

A cyber threat intelligence process collects, analyses and evaluates threat information including data breaches and misleading information about the institution on the Internet, social media and dark web
Flagged anomalous activities are investigated and responded to according to their complexity

Cyber crisis management policies and procedures incorporate attack scenarios and responses into the crisis management plan, escalation, BCP and DR, with a communication plan for shareholders, regulators, customers and employees

A Cyber Incident Response Plan covers preparedness (CERT governance, reporting, roles, invocation and escalation), detection and analysis (points of compromise, damage assessment including threat-actor claims, evidence preservation), containment and eradication, recovery with contingency strategies, and post-incident review with lessons learned
CERT members are conversant with the incident response plan and procedures and remain contactable at all times
A secure, reliable out-of-band communication infrastructure for internal and external stakeholders operates if primary communications are compromised

An annual cyber drill tests the CIRP and out-of-band communications on current and emerging scenarios with the board, senior management and relevant third parties, covering escalation, communication and decision-making at different impact levels and the readiness of CERT and third parties; results are reported to the board

Loss provision arrangements are reviewed against scenario analysis of extreme cyber events; any cyber insurance adequately covers the events and liabilities, its warranties and obligations are reflected in crisis procedures without unintended exclusions, and insurer obligations do not impair acting in the institution's and customers' best interests
Cyber incidents are notified to the Bank per the Operational Risk Reporting, Business Continuity Management and Merchant Acquiring Services policy documents and any other specified policy
Cyber threat intelligence is shared with the industry on a timely basis via the Bank's, industry's or law enforcement platforms, with resources allocated to industry-wide intelligence initiatives

A cyber resilience framework (CRF) articulates governance, resilience objectives and risk tolerance against the evolving threat environment, targets operational resilience against extreme but plausible attacks, and supports identification, protection, detection, response and recovery of on-premises and third-party-hosted systems and data
The institution collaborates and cooperates closely with relevant stakeholders and authorities in combating cyber threats

The CRF includes institutional understanding of cyber risk context and posture; identification, classification and prioritisation of critical systems, information, assets and interconnectivity; threats, vulnerabilities and countermeasures; layered defence with zero-trust, micro-segmentation and security by design; continuous surveillance for timely detection; incident handling procedures and a crisis response playbook; secure information sharing with other institutions and FMIs; a centralised automated technology asset inventory; and a cyber risk management function escalating high-risk threats to senior management and the board
As a designated National Critical Information Infrastructure entity, the institution complies with the Cyber Security Act 2024 requirements, guidelines and NACSA directives and standards
The Appendix 5 control measures are adopted to enhance resilience to cyber attacks
A realistic red-team simulation attack on the infrastructure is conducted at least once every three years

Cybersecurity operations have clear responsibilities with mitigating measures for each phase of the attack life cycle: reconnaissance, weaponisation, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, exfiltration

Continuous proactive monitoring and timely detection of anomalies via a Security Operations Centre with competent resources and tools, covering all critical systems and supporting infrastructure, with regular vulnerability assessment and penetration testing per Appendix 5

The CRF implements robust security controls for digital services: minimum controls per delivery channel assessed regularly (Appendices 2, 3, 4, 11), proper user and device authentication and transaction authorisation against impersonation and fraud (Appendix 3), and strong physical and logical controls

Where the §12 digital services controls are not yet implemented, documented explanation shows alternatives are at least as effective and the institution assumes liability for fraud arising from the gap

The CRF extends to customers' mobile devices and access points: layered controls protecting the mobile application and its data, continuous surveillance of exploitation with swift control upgrades, incident handling to help customers contain damage, coordinated rapid countermeasure upgrades across functions, senior management review with escalation thresholds, and board apprisal of outcomes
Fraud detection capabilities and rules are updated promptly on new modus operandi, supported by risk analytics and continuous upgrade per Appendix 11 Fraud Detection Standards

Digital service delivery risks are mitigated: secure communication channels with compensating controls for phishing-prone channels (no clickable links in SMS), advance customer information on new controls, and practical ways for customers to verify calls from the institution or its outsourced providers
Customers can manage activation and de-activation of payment cards for card-not-present and overseas transactions, without diminishing the institution's liabilities and duty of care

Customer awareness programmes are continuously reviewed for effectiveness: timely practical fraud-identification information including new modus operandi, clear explanation of security measures and how to verify genuine sites and apps, real-time alerts when measures are absent, and measures such as interactive simulations

Customers can conveniently report, suspend and re-activate accounts on suspected fraud: a secure self-service kill switch, an adequately resourced contact centre, and restoration of access within a reasonable time after validation

Incidents involving potential fraud or compromised customer data trigger heightened monitoring of affected accounts, notification of affected customers with mitigation information, and revocation and re-issue of affected credentials or payment instruments where exploitation risk exists
Scope, frequency and intensity of technology audits are commensurate with the complexity, sophistication and criticality of systems and applications

The technology audit plan is reviewed annually with appropriate frequency and coverage of critical services, third-party providers, material external interfaces, delayed or terminated critical projects, and post-implementation reviews of new or material enhancements
Internal audit has dedicated, specialised, professionally certified technology audit resources conversant with the institution's systems and delivery channels

A technically competent external provider performs a production data centre resilience and risk assessment (DCRA) at least every three years or on material change, covering paragraphs 10.24–10.28; reliance on third-party reports for provider-managed data centres is consistent with risk appetite and meets the same requirements; the board-level committee deliberates the outcome

A technically competent external provider performs network resilience and risk assessments (NRA) at least every three years or on material network design change, covering paragraphs 10.36–10.43; the board-level committee deliberates the outcome

Regular technology and cybersecurity awareness education for all staff is conducted at least annually, reflects the evolving threat landscape, is measured for effectiveness, and includes third-party providers where appropriate
Staff in technology operations, cybersecurity and risk management receive adequate continuous training and are competent and suitably certified
Board members receive regular training and information on technology developments to discharge their oversight role

The board establishes and approves a technology risk appetite aligned with the institution's risk appetite: risk tolerances for technology events, a risk owner and residual-risk acceptance criteria and authority, key risk indicators, sufficient resources, and regular review

The board approves and reviews IT and cybersecurity strategic plans of at least three years, endorses and oversees the TRMF and CRF, requires robust risk assessments for critical systems and emerging technology, has IT frameworks and policies reviewed at least every three years, and ensures the framework supports technology applications to the Bank
A board-level committee with at least one member with technology experience and competencies oversees technology matters

The board obtains regular updates on technology and cyber threats, allocates time to discuss cyber risks including extreme-incident impacts with external expert input where appropriate, and participates in cybersecurity awareness and training

The board audit committee ensures the effectiveness of the internal technology audit function: competent audit staff, appropriate scope, procedures and frequency, and prompt closure of corrective actions

Senior management implements the TRMF and CRF as policies and procedures consistent with risk appetite, ensures the crisis management plan escalates recovery considering duration, customers affected and transactions impacted, and reports KPIs and risk controls to the board regularly

A cross-functional committee of cyber, technology and business senior management oversees the strategic technology plan and policies, updates the board on key technology matters, and approves policy deviations after risk assessment, reporting material deviations to the board
The technology risk management framework (TRMF) is an integral part of the enterprise risk management framework

The TRMF defines technology risk, assigns responsibilities with governance and reporting, identifies risks including emerging technology, classifies all information assets by criticality, sets measurement and assessment methods, controls and mitigations, continuous monitoring, an accurate risk profile, key resources and interdependencies including critical third parties and their connected parties, scenario analysis for severe conditions, and incident management to restore services to a secure and stable state

An independent enterprise-wide technology risk management function implements the TRMF and CRF, advises on critical technology projects and escalates critical issues, and gives independent views on third-party assessments

A designated CISO with sufficient authority, independence and resources is independent of day-to-day operations, apprises the board and senior management of current and emerging technology risks, has the requisite technical, audit, governance, risk, strategic and third-party-risk skills, and is appropriately certified

The CISO formulates policies implementing the TRMF and CRF, enforces compliance with them and with technology regulatory requirements, and advises senior management on technology risk and security matters

As part of their ICT security policies, procedures, protocols, and tools referred to in Article 9(2) of Regulation (EU) 2022/2554, financial entities shall develop, document, and implement a policy on encryption and cryptographic controls.
the encryption of data at rest and in transit;

Financial entities shall include in the policy on encryption and cryptographic controls referred to in paragraph 1 criteria for the selection of cryptographic techniques and use practices, taking into account leading practices, and standards as defined in Article 2, point (1), of Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012, and the classification of relevant ICT assets established in accordance with Article 8(1) of Regulation (EU) 2022/2554. Financial entities that are not able to adhere to the leading practices or standards, or to use the most reliable techniques, shall adopt mitigation and monitoring measures that ensure resilience against cyber threats.

Financial entities shall include in the policy on encryption and cryptographic controls referred to in paragraph 1 provisions for updating or changing, where necessary, the cryptographic technology on the basis of developments in cryptanalysis. Those updates or changes shall ensure that the cryptographic technology remains resilient against cyber threats, as required by Article 10(2), point (a). Financial entities that are not able to update or change the cryptographic technology shall adopt mitigation and monitoring measures that ensure resilience against cyber threats.

Financial entities shall include in the policy on encryption and cryptographic controls referred to in paragraph 1 a requirement to record the adoption of mitigation and monitoring measures adopted in accordance with paragraphs 3 and 4 and to provide a reasoned explanation for doing so.

Financial entities shall include in the cryptographic key management policy referred to in Article 6(2), point (d), requirements for managing cryptographic keys through their whole lifecycle, including generating, renewing, storing, backing up, archiving, retrieving, transmitting, retiring, revoking, and destroying those cryptographic keys.

Financial entities shall identify and implement controls to protect cryptographic keys through their whole lifecycle against loss, unauthorised access, disclosure, and modification. Financial entities shall design those controls on the basis of the results of the approved data classification and the ICT risk assessment.
Financial entities shall develop and implement methods to replace the cryptographic keys in the case of loss, or where those keys are compromised or damaged.

Financial entities shall create and maintain a register for all certificates and certificate-storing devices for at least ICT assets supporting critical or important functions. Financial entities shall keep that register up to date.
Financial entities shall ensure the prompt renewal of certificates in advance of their expiration.

As part of the ICT security policies, procedures, protocols, and tools referred to in Article 9(2) of Regulation (EU) 2022/2554, financial entities shall develop, document, and implement vulnerability management procedures.
identify and update relevant and trustworthy information resources to build and maintain awareness about vulnerabilities;

ensure the performance of automated vulnerability scanning and assessments on ICT assets, whereby the frequency and scope of those activities shall be commensurate to the classification established in accordance with Article 8(1) of Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 and the overall risk profile of the ICT asset; [Second subparagraph:] For the purposes of point (b), financial entities shall perform the automated vulnerability scanning and assessments on ICT assets for the ICT assets supporting critical or important functions on at least a weekly basis.

track the usage of: (i) third-party libraries, including open-source libraries, used by ICT services supporting critical or important functions; (ii) ICT services developed by the financial entity itself or specifically customised or developed for the financial entity by an ICT third-party service provider; [Fourth subparagraph:] For the purposes of point (d), financial entities shall, where appropriate in collaboration with the ICT third-party service provider, monitor the version and possible updates of the third-party libraries. As part of the ICT security policies, procedures, protocols, and tools referred to in Article 9(2) of Regulation (EU) 2022/2554, financial entities shall develop, document and implement patch management procedures.

As part of the ICT security policies, procedures, protocols, and tools referred to in Article 9(2) of Regulation (EU) 2022/2554, financial entities shall develop, document, and implement a data and system security procedure.

the identification of security measures to ensure that only authorised software is installed in ICT systems and endpoint devices;

for ICT assets or services operated by an ICT third-party service provider, the identification and implementation of requirements to maintain digital operational resilience, in accordance with the results of the data classification and ICT risk assessment. IT control policies setting the ground rules for IT controls are developed by senior management, formally approved by the Board or its committee, and implemented across IT functions and business units

Mechanisms (periodic reminders, orientation for new recruits) promote regular awareness of IT control policies
An IT organisation structure and job descriptions for IT functions are documented and approved by senior management

Segregation of duties within and among IT functions is enforced (developers have no production access; security management has no conflicting duties), with compensating controls such as peer review where segregation is impractical
An IT planning or steering committee of senior management, business units and IT meets regularly and reports major technology initiatives and material IT issues to senior management and the Board
A documented IT strategy covering long- and short-term initiatives is endorsed by the Board and senior management and reviewed at least annually
The function responsible for the technology risk management (TRM) process is clearly established

The TRM function assists business units and IT in identifying, measuring, monitoring and controlling technology risks, promotes policy compliance and supports investigation of technology-related frauds and incidents

A formal technology risk acknowledgement and acceptance process reviews, evaluates and approves major non-compliance with IT control policies: risk description and assessment, mitigating controls, remedial plan, approval by the risk owner and senior management
Technology audits periodically assess the TRM process and IT controls under an annual technology audit plan; audit issues are recorded, followed up and rectified
Where in-house technology audit expertise is insufficient it is supplemented by external specialists or group technology auditors
Staff of IT functions, the TRM function and technology audit are competent, with sufficient staffing for present and expected demand and turnover
A process identifies material skill gaps against a skill matrix and an adequate training programme is in place; professional qualifications are encouraged for security, TRM and audit staff
Respective responsibilities of local and overseas offices for IT controls and support are clearly set out in policies, procedures or service agreements
Each application system has an assigned information owner accountable for confidentiality and integrity, working with the TRM and IT functions
Information is classified by sensitivity with guidelines, definitions and protection procedures for each class
Confidentiality is protected regardless of media; secure disposal and destruction processes exist for sensitive paper and electronic media

Cryptography uses industry-accepted solutions with sound key management: secure generation, distribution, storage, entry, use and archiving (tamper-resistant storage recommended) and off-site backup of keys under equivalent controls
Access to information and application systems is restricted by authentication and access control rules; every user has a unique ID with an appropriate authentication method

Effective password rules avoid easy-to-guess passwords and enforce periodic change; multi-factor authentication is used for higher-risk transactions and activities (payments, financial messages, mobile computing)
Privileged and emergency IDs are granted only necessary authorities, formally approved before release, monitored (peer review of logs), safeguarded, and have passwords changed immediately on return

A security administration function grants, changes and removes access with information-owner approval, removes rights on leaving or role change, re-certifies user access periodically (e.g. annually), reviews security logs and violation reports timely, and performs incident analysis, reporting and investigation
Segregation of duties or compensating controls within the security administration function mitigate unauthorised activity by that function
Incident response and reporting procedures handle security incidents during and outside office hours and include timely reporting to the HKMA of confirmed IT-related fraud or major security breaches

Baseline security requirements safeguard applications, operating systems, system software and databases: authenticated and authorised access, periodic static-data integrity checks, secure configuration with unnecessary services removed, timely vendor patching with clear responsibility, documented configurations with periodic certification, and protected logging and monitoring of system and user activity
End-user computing is controlled: data security, documentation, storage and backup, recovery, audit responsibilities and training

Mobile computing controls cover user approval, remote-access authentication, protection of devices against theft and malware, encryption of sensitive data in the mobile environment and in transit, and backup of mobile data

Malicious-software controls prohibit unauthorised downloads and doubtful sites, keep reputable anti-virus current, block executables and mobile code with known vulnerabilities, and scan all devices regularly with recovery procedures

Critical information processing facilities sit in secure areas with security barriers and entry controls; access is restricted to authorised personnel and reviewed regularly; buildings give minimum indication of purpose
Data centre sites consider environmental threats; environmental monitoring (fire, smoke, temperature, water, dust) and protection from power failure (UPS, backup generator) are in place
Third-party access to secure areas is approved and monitored; recruitment of permanent and temporary technology staff and contractors includes verification and background checks

A project management framework specifies the methodology for major technology projects: responsibilities, activity breakdown, time and resource budgets, milestones, checkpoints, dependencies, quality assurance, risk assessment and approvals

A full project life-cycle methodology governs development, implementation and maintenance of major systems from initiation through feasibility, requirements, design, development, testing, training, implementation, operation and maintenance
The life-cycle methodology defines roles and deliverables per phase and ensures security requirements are identified with business requirements, built, tested and implemented
An independent party (QA, TRM or technology audit) conducts a quality assurance review of major projects for compliance with the methodology, policies, control requirements, regulations and law

A formal acceptance process promotes only tested and approved systems to production; testing is in a separate environment; production data is not used in testing unless de-sensitised and approved by the information owner; performance testing precedes promotion
A formal software package acquisition process evaluates the package (licence, functionality, performance, security) and the supplier (financial condition, reputation, technical capability)
Ongoing maintenance and support of software packages are specified in formal contracts; escrow is considered for mission-critical packages

A formal change management process covers classification and impact, roles with segregation of duties so no one person can change production unreviewed, version control and audit trails, scheduling and tracking, rollback, and post-implementation verification
Emergency changes follow formal procedures and are approved by the information owner and relevant parties at the time, or endorsed by the information owner as soon as practicable afterwards
Emergency changes are logged and backed up (previous and changed versions and data), reviewed by independent personnel, and replaced by proper fixes through normal change management
Service level agreements with business units cover availability, performance, capacity for growth and user support, with procedures to manage delivery
An IT operations manual documents operator tasks, job scheduling and execution, and on-site and off-site backup of data and software (frequency, scope, retention) for production and development
A problem management system responds to IT operational incidents, escalates to IT management, and records, analyses and tracks incidents to rectification; a helpdesk provides front-line support
Application performance is continuously monitored with timely exception reporting and forecasting to identify problems early and feed capacity planning
Capacity planning covers backup systems and related facilities as well as production
IT facilities and equipment are maintained per industry practice and supplier intervals, with fault and maintenance records and a hardware and facility inventory of purchased and leased assets
An IT disaster recovery plan ensures critical application systems and technology services resume per business recovery requirements (TM-G-2), with adequate insurance of IT resources
Network management responsibility is assigned to skilled, resourced individuals; network standards, design, diagrams and procedures are documented, current, communicated and reviewed periodically
Critical communications facilities are identified and single points of failure minimised by automatic re-routing, multiple exchanges and alternate telecommunications providers
The network is monitored continuously: services and performance against targets, traffic volumes and bottlenecks, and detection of unusual activity based on attack characteristics
Powerful network analysis and monitoring tools are protected from unauthorised use and restricted to authorised staff under approval and review
Procedures for use of networks and network services define available services, authorisation of who may access them, and protection of access points, connections and services

Internal networks are segregated by access-control need; production systems sit in dedicated segments separated from internet, extranet and market-data traffic; sensitive inter-segment traffic is controlled and tamper-protected

WLAN policies cover approval, installation, operation and administration; a risk assessment of accessible information precedes implementation; a standard WLAN security configuration and network certification apply

A technology and cyber risk management framework proportionate to the nature, scale and complexity of operations is in place, consistent with IC-1 and TM-G-1

General. Contractors will protect all classified information that they are provided access to or that they possess. This responsibility applies at both contractor and USG locations.
Contractor Security Officials. Contractors will appoint security officials who are U.S. citizens, except in exceptional circumstances (see § 117.9(m) and § 117.11(e)).

Oversee the implementation of the requirements of this rule. Depending upon the size and complexity of the contractor's security operations, a single contractor employee may serve in more than one position.
Undergo the same security training that is required for all other contractor employees pursuant to § 117.12, in addition to their position specific training.
Be designated in writing with their designation documented in accordance with CSA guidance.

Undergo a personnel security investigation and national security eligibility determination for access to classified information at the level of the entity's eligibility determination for access to classified information ( e.g., FCL level) and be on the KMP list for the cleared entity.
Ensure the contractor maintains a system of security controls in accordance with the requirements of this rule.

Appoint a contractor employee or employees, in writing, as the FSO and appoint the same employee or a different employee as the ITPSO. The SMO may appoint a single employee for both roles or may appoint one employee as the FSO and a different employee as the ITPSO.
Remain fully informed of the facility's classified operations.

Make decisions based on classified threat reporting and their thorough knowledge, understanding, and appreciation of the threat information and the potential impacts caused by a loss of classified information.
Retain accountability for the management and operations of the facility without delegating that accountability to a subordinate manager.

Supervise and direct security measures necessary for implementing the applicable requirements of this rule and the related USG security requirements to ensure the protection of classified information.
Complete security training pursuant to § 117.12 and as deemed appropriate by the CSA.
ITPSO. The ITPSO will establish and execute an insider threat program.
If the appointed ITPSO is not also the FSO, the ITPSO will ensure that the FSO is an integral member of the contractor's insider threat program.
The ITPSO will complete training pursuant to § 117.12.

An entity family may choose to establish an entity family-wide insider threat program with one senior official appointed, in writing, to establish, and execute the program as the ITPSO. Each cleared entity using the entity-wide ITPSO must separately appoint that person as its ITPSO for that facility. The ITPSO will provide an implementation plan to the CSA for executing the insider threat program across the entity family.

ISSM. Contractors who are, or will be, processing classified information on an information system located at the contractor facility will appoint an employee to serve as the ISSM. The ISSM must be eligible for access to classified information to the highest level of the information processed on the system(s) under their responsibility. The contractor will ensure that the ISSM is adequately trained and possesses technical competence commensurate with the complexity of the contractor's classified information system. The contractor will notify the applicable CSA if there is a change in the ISSM. The ISSM will oversee development, implementation, and evaluation of the contractor's classified information system program. ISSM responsibilities are in § 117.18.

Employees performing security duties. Those employees whose official duties include performance of NISP-related security functions will complete security training tailored to the security functions performed. This training requirement also applies to consultants whose official duties include security functions.

Other KMP. In addition to the SMO, the FSO, and the ITPSO, the contractor will include on the KMP list, subject to CSA concurrence, any other officials who either hold majority interest or stock in the entity, or who have direct or indirect authority to influence or decide issues affecting the management or operations of the contractor or issues affecting classified contract performance. The CSA may either:

Allow the entity to formally exclude these KMP from access to classified information. The entity's governing board will affirm the exclusion by issuing a formal action (see table), and provide a copy of the exclusion action to the CSA. The entity's governing board will document this exclusion action.

Insider Threat Program. Pursuant to this rule and CSA provided guidance to supplement unique CSA mission requirements, the contractor will establish and maintain an insider threat program to gather, integrate, and report relevant and available information indicative of a potential or actual insider threat, consistent with E.O. 13587 and Presidential Memorandum “National Insider Threat Policy and Minimum Standards for Executive Branch Insider Threat Programs.”

Standard practice procedures. The contractor will implement all applicable provisions of this rule at each of its cleared facility locations. The contractor will prepare written procedures when the CSA determines them to be necessary to reasonably exclude the possibility of loss or compromise of classified information, and in accordance with additional CSA-provided guidance, as applicable.

Cooperation with Federal agencies. Contractors will cooperate with Federal agencies and their officially credentialed USG or contractor representatives during official reviews, investigations concerning the protection of classified information, or personnel security investigations of present or former employees and others ( e.g., consultants or visitors). At a minimum, cooperation includes:

Security training and briefings. Contractors will advise all cleared employees, including those assigned to USG locations or operations outside the United States, of their individual responsibility for classification management and for safeguarding classified information. Contractors will provide security training to cleared employees consisting of initial briefings, refresher briefings, and debriefings in accordance with § 117.12.

Contractor reviews. Contractors will review their security programs on a continuing basis and conduct a formal self-inspection at least annually and at intervals consistent with risk management principles.

Self-inspections will include the review of the classified activity, classified information, classified information systems, conditions of the overall security program, and the insider threat program. They will have sufficient scope, depth, and frequency, and will have management support during the self-inspection and during remedial actions taken as a result of the self-inspection. Self-inspections will include the review of samples representing the contractor's derivative classification actions, as applicable.

The contractor will prepare a formal report describing the self-inspection, its findings, and its resolution of issues discovered during the self-inspection. The contractor will retain the formal report for CSA review until after the next CSA security review is completed.

The SMO at the cleared facility will annually certify to the CSA, in writing, that a self-inspection has been conducted, that other KMP have been briefed on the results of the self-inspection, that appropriate corrective actions have been taken, and that management fully supports the security program at the cleared facility in the manner as described in the certification.

Contractors working at USG locations. Contractor employees performing work within the confines of a USG facility will safeguard classified information according to the procedures of the host installation or agency.

Hotlines. Federal agencies maintain hotlines to provide an unconstrained avenue for USG and contractor employees to report, without fear of reprisal, known or suspected instances of security irregularities and infractions concerning contracts, programs, or projects. These hotlines do not supplant the contractor's responsibility to facilitate reporting and timely investigations of security issues concerning its operations or personnel. Contractor personnel are encouraged to report information through established contractor channels. The hotline may be used as an alternate means to report this type of information. Contractors will inform all personnel that hotlines may be used for reporting issues of national security significance. Each CSA will post hotline information and telephone numbers on their websites for contractor access.
Rule interpretations. Contractors will forward requests for interpretations of this rule to their CSA in accordance with their CSA-provided guidance to supplement unique CSA mission requirements.

Waivers to this rule. Contractors will submit any requests to waive provisions of this rule in accordance with CSA procedures, which may include periodic review of approved waivers. When submitting a request for a waiver, the contractor will, in writing, explain why it is impractical or unreasonable for the contractor to comply with the requirement it is asking to waive, identify alternative measures as prescribed by this rule, and include a proposed duration for the waiver. The contractor cannot implement a waiver unless the waiver is approved by the applicable CSA.

Report certain events that may have an effect on the status of the entity's or an employee's eligibility for access to classified information; report events that indicate an insider threat to classified information or to employees with access to classified information; report events that affect proper safeguarding of classified information; and report events that indicate classified information has been, or is suspected to be, lost or compromised.
Provide reports to the FBI, or other Federal authorities as required by this rule, the terms of a classified contract or other agreement, and by U.S. law.
Provide complete information to enable the CSA to ascertain whether classified information is adequately protected.
Submit reports to the FBI, the CSA, or the ISOO as specified in paragraphs (b), (c), and (g) of this section.
Appropriately mark reports containing classified information in accordance with § 117.14.

Clearly mark a report containing information submitted in confidence as containing that information. When reports contain information pertaining to an individual, 5 U.S.C. 552a (also known as and referred to in this rule as “The Privacy Act of 1974, as amended,”) permits the withholding of certain information from the individual in accordance with specific exemptions, which include authority to withhold release of information to the extent that the disclosure of the information would reveal the identity of a source who furnished the information to the USG under an express promise that the identity of the source would be held in confidence.

Reports to be submitted to the FBI. The contractor will promptly submit a written report to the nearest field office of the FBI regarding information coming to the contractor's attention concerning actual, probable, or possible espionage, sabotage, terrorism, or subversive activities at any of its locations.
An initial report may be made by phone, but it must be followed up in writing ( e.g., email or formal correspondence), regardless of the FBI's disposition of the report.
The contractor will promptly notify the CSA when they make a report to the FBI and provide the CSA a copy of the written report.

Adverse information. Contractors are required to report adverse information coming to their attention concerning any of their employees determined to be eligible for access to classified information, in accordance with this rule, SEAD 3, and CSA-provided guidance. Contractors will not make reports based on rumor or innuendo.

The termination of employment of an employee does not negate the requirement to submit this report. If a contractor employee is assigned to a USG location, the contractor will furnish a copy of the report and its final disposition to the USG security point of contact for that location.

Suspicious contacts. Contractors will report information pertaining to suspicious contacts with employees determined to be eligible for access to classified information, and pertaining to efforts to obtain illegal or unauthorized access to the contractor's cleared facility by any means, including:

Change in status of employees determined eligible for access to classified information. Contractors will report by means of the CSA-designated reporting mechanism information pertaining to changes in status of employees determined eligible for access to classified information such as:
Citizenship by naturalization. Contractors will report if a non-U.S. citizen employee granted an LAA becomes a citizen through naturalization. The report will include:

Employees desiring not to be processed for a national security eligibility determination or not to perform classified work. Contractors will report instances when an employee no longer wishes to be processed for a determination of eligibility for access to classified information or to continue having access to classified information, and the reason for that request.

Classified information nondisclosure agreement (NDA). Contractors will report the refusal by an employee to sign the SF 312, “Classified Information Nondisclosure Agreement,” (available at: https://www.gsa.gov/cdnstatic/SF312-13.pdf?forceDownload=1 ) or other approved NDA.
Change of ownership or control of the contractor, including stock transfers that affect control of the entity.
Change of operating name or address of the entity or any of its locations determined eligible for access to classified information.

Any change to the information previously submitted for KMP including, as appropriate, the names of the individuals the contractor is replacing. A new complete KMP listing need be submitted only at the discretion of the contractor or when requested by the CSA. The contractor will provide a statement indicating:

Any action to terminate business or operations for any reason, imminent adjudication or reorganization in bankruptcy, or any change that might affect the validity of the contractor's eligibility for access to classified information.

Any material change concerning the information previously reported concerning foreign ownership, control, or influence (FOCI). This report will be made by the submission of an updated SF 328, “Certificate Pertaining to Foreign Interests,” in accordance with CSA-provided guidance. When submitting this information, it is not necessary to repeat answers that have not changed. When entering into discussion, consultations, or agreements that may reasonably lead to effective ownership or control by a foreign interest, the contractor will report the details to the CSA in writing. If the contractor has received a Schedule 13D from the investor, the contractor will forward a copy with the report.
Changes in storage capability. The contractor will report any changes in their storage requirement or capability to safeguard classified material.
Inability to safeguard classified material. The contractor will report any emergency situation that renders their location incapable of safeguarding classified material as soon as possible.

Prime contractors, including subcontractors who have in turn subcontracted work, will report any information coming to their attention that may indicate that classified information cannot be adequately protected by a subcontractor, or other circumstances that may impact the validity of the eligibility for access to classified information of any subcontractors.

Subcontractors will report any information coming to their attention that may indicate that classified information cannot be adequately protected or other circumstances that may impact the validity of the eligibility for access to classified information of their prime contractor.

Dispositioned material previously terminated. The contractor will make a report when the location or disposition of material previously terminated from accountability is subsequently discovered and brought back into accountability.
Foreign classified contracts. Contractors will report any pre-contract negotiation or award not placed through a CSA or U.S. GCA that involves, or may involve:

Reporting of improper receipt of foreign government material. The contractor will report to the CSA the receipt of classified material from foreign interests that is not received through USG channels.

Reporting by subcontractor. Subcontractors will also notify their prime contractors if they make any reports to their CSA in accordance with the provisions of paragraphs (c)(7) through (c)(10) of this section.

Reports of loss, compromise, or suspected compromise. The contractor will report any loss, compromise, or suspected compromise of classified information, U.S. or foreign, to the CSA in accordance with paragraph (d)(1) through (d)(3) of this section. Each CSA may provide additional guidance concerning the reporting time period. If the contractor is located on a USG facility, the contractor will submit the report to the CSA and to the head of the USG facility.

Preliminary inquiry. Immediately upon receipt of a security violation report involving classified information, the contractor will initiate a preliminary inquiry to ascertain all of the circumstances surrounding the presumed loss, compromise, or suspected compromise, including validation of the classification of the information.

Initial report. If the contractor's preliminary inquiry confirms that a loss, compromise, or suspected compromise of any classified information occurred, the contractor will promptly submit an initial report of the incident unless otherwise notified by the CSA.

Final report. When the investigation has been completed, the contractor will submit a final report to the CSA which, in turn, will follow CSA procedures to notify the applicable GCA. The report will include:

Employee information in compromise cases. When requested by the CSA, the contractor will report information concerning an employee or other individual, determined to be responsible for the incident, when the information is needed by the CSA for the loss, compromise, or suspected compromise of classified information.

Individual culpability reports. Contractors will establish and enforce policies that provide for appropriate administrative or disciplinary actions taken against employees who violate the requirements of this rule.

Contractors will establish a system to manage and track information regarding employees with eligibility for access to classified information who violate the requirements of this rule in order to be able to identify patterns of negligence or carelessness, or to identify a potential insider threat.

Contractors will establish and apply a graduated scale of administrative and disciplinary actions in the event of employee security violations or negligence in the handling of classified information. CSAs may provide guidance to contractors with examples of administrative or disciplinary actions that the contractor may consider implementing in the event of employee violations or negligence. Contractors are required to submit a final report to the CSA with the findings of an employee's culpability and what corrective actions were taken.

Contractors will include a statement of the administrative or disciplinary actions taken against an employee in a final report to the CSA. A statement must be included when the individual responsible for a security violation can be determined. Contractors' final reports will indicate whether one or more of the following factors are evident:

Reports to be submitted to the designated DoD CSO. CDCs will immediately report to the DoD CSO, any cyber incident on a classified covered information system that has been approved by that CSO to process classified information.
At a minimum, the report will include:
Reports involving classified foreign government information will be reported to the Director, Defense Technology Security Administration (DoD).

Reports on non-Federal information systems not authorized to process classified information. CDCs will report cyber incidents on non-Federal, unclassified information systems in accordance with contract requirements.

The CDC will allow, upon request by DoD personnel, access by DoD personnel to additional equipment or information of the CDC that is necessary to conduct forensic analysis of reportable cyber incidents in addition to any analysis conducted by the CDC.
Contractors will report instances of redundant or duplicative security review and audit activity by the CSAs to the Director, ISOO, for resolution.

Contractors will report instances of CSAs duplicating processing to determine an entity's eligibility for access to classified information when there is an existing determination of an entity's eligibility for access to classified information by another CSA.
Neither the contractor nor its employees will be permitted access to classified information until the CSA has made an entity eligibility determination ( e.g., issued an FCL).

The requirement for a favorable entity eligibility determination (also referred to in some instances as an FCL) for a prime contractor includes instances where all access to classified information will be limited to subcontractors. A prime contractor must have a favorable entity eligibility determination at the same or higher classification level as its subcontractors.

A contractor will not use its favorable entity eligibility determination for advertising or promotional purposes. This does not prohibit the contractor from advertising employee positions that require a PCL in connection with the position.

A contractor or prospective contractor cannot apply for its own entity eligibility determination. A GCA or a currently cleared contractor may sponsor an entity for an entity eligibility determination at any point during the contracting or agreement life cycle at which the entity must have access to classified information to participate (including the solicitation or competition phase).

Need access to classified information in connection with a legitimate USG or foreign government requirement, and access must be consistent with U.S. national security interests as determined by the CSA.
Be organized and existing:

Have a record of integrity and lawful conduct in its business dealings.

Have a SMO, FSO, and ITPSO who have and who maintain eligibility for access to classified information and are not excluded from participating in USG contracts or agreements in accordance with § 117.7(b)(1) through § 117.7(b)(3).
Not be under FOCI to such a degree that a favorable entity eligibility determination for access to classified information would be inconsistent with the national interest, in the judgment of the CSA.
Maintain sufficient authorized and cleared employees to manage and implement the requirements of this rule in accordance with CSA guidance.
Not pose an unacceptable risk to national security interests, in the judgment of the CSA.
Meet all requirements governing access to classified information established by the CSA or the relevant authorizing law, regulation, or government-wide policy.
Provide CSA-requested documentation within timelines established by the CSA.
Have and identify the SMO.
Appoint a U.S. citizen employee as the FSO.
Appoint a U.S. citizen employee as the ITPSO.

Submit requests for personnel security investigations for the SMO, FSO, ITPSO, and those other KMP identified by the CSA as requiring eligibility for access to classified information in connection with the entity eligibility.

Exclusion procedures. If a CSA determines that certain KMP can be excluded from access to classified information, the contractor will follow the procedures in accordance with § 117.7(b)(5)(ii).

The SMO or other KMP are not appointed as the FSO or ITPSO. FSOs and ITPSOs may not be temporarily excluded. A cleared employee must always be appointed to fulfill the requirements of these positions in accordance with this rule.

An employee, cleared to the level of the entity eligibility determination, must be able to fulfill the NISP responsibilities of the temporarily excluded KMP in accordance with this rule while the temporary exclusion is in effect.
The contractor's governing board affirms the exclusion action, and provides a copy of the exclusion action to the CSA. The organization's governing body will document this action.

Multiple facility organizations. The home office must have an entity eligibility determination at the same level as the highest entity eligibility determination of an entity within the MFO. The CSA will determine whether branch offices are eligible for access to classified information if the branch offices need access and meet all other requirements.

The joint venture must be established as a legal business entity ( e.g. limited liability company, corporation, or partnership). A joint venture established by contract that is not also established as a legal business entity is not eligible for an entity eligibility determination.

The business entity operating as a joint venture must have been awarded a classified contract or sponsored by a GCA or prime contractor for an entity eligibility determination in advance of a potential award for which the business entity has bid pursuant to paragraph (c) of this section.
The business entity operating as a joint venture must have an employee or employees appointed as security officials or KMP pursuant to § 117.7(b).
The entity must otherwise meet the entity eligibility determination requirements set out in this rule.

Termination of the entity eligibility determination. Once granted, a favorable entity eligibility determination remains in effect until terminated or revoked. If the entity eligibility determination is terminated or revoked, the contractor will return all classified material in its possession to the appropriate GCA or dispose of the material as instructed by the CSA. The contractor should be aware that it may request an administrative termination or the CSA may:

Records maintenance. Contractors will maintain the original CSA designated forms for the duration of the entity eligibility determination in accordance with CSA-provided guidance.
The contractor must determine that access to classified information is essential in the performance of tasks or services related to the fulfillment of a classified contract.

The contractor will immediately deny access to classified information to any employee when notified of a denial, revocation, or suspension of eligibility regardless of the contractor employee's location.

Contractors will annotate and maintain the accuracy of their employees' records in the system of record for contractor eligibility and access to classified information, when one has been designated by the CSA.

The contractor will limit requests for determinations of eligibility for access to classified information to the minimum number of employees and consultants necessary for operational efficiency in accordance with contractual obligations and other requirements of this rule. Contractors will not submit requests for determination of eligibility for access to classified information for individuals who are not their employees or consultants; nor will they submit requests for employees of subcontractors.

Financial disclosure. When a GCA requires that a contractor employee complete a financial disclosure form, the contractor will ensure that the employee has the opportunity to complete and submit the form in accordance with the Privacy Act of 1974, as amended, and other applicable provisions of law.

Reinvestigation and Continuous Evaluation.
